title: Virtual threads & structured concurrency
scopeHtml: Project Loom model, carriers and continuations, pinning across Java 21/24/25, ThreadLocal vs ScopedValue, structured concurrency status, bounding concurrency, Spring/Tomcat enablement, observability and migration risks. Version facts (checked against JEP 444, 491, 505, 506 and the JDK 21 docs): virtual threads final in 21; synchronized pinning removed in 24 (JEP 491); ScopedValue final in 25 (JEP 506); StructuredTaskScope still preview in 25 (JEP 505, fifth preview).

questions.promptHtml: What is a virtual thread, and how is it different from a platform thread?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand the model (cheap, JVM-scheduled threads) rather than repeating "lightweight threads, faster".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A platform thread is a thin wrapper over one OS thread, with a roughly fixed stack reserved by the OS and a scheduler in the kernel. A virtual thread is a java.lang.Thread implemented by the JVM: its stack lives on the heap, and the JDK schedules it onto a small pool of platform threads called carriers. It is final in Java 21. It doesn't run faster; it lets me have hundreds of thousands of blocked-waiting threads, so thread-per-request scales with I/O concurrency again."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A platform thread costs an OS thread: typically about 1 MB of stack address space reserved (-Xss/ThreadStackSize, platform default, verify per OS), kernel scheduling, context-switch cost, and a hard practical ceiling of a few thousand threads. A service doing 10 blocking HTTP calls per request therefore tops out around "pool size / latency" requests per second no matter how idle the CPU is.

A virtual thread is still a Thread (same API, same Thread.currentThread(), same stack traces), but:

Aspect Platform thread Virtual thread
Backed by 1:1 OS thread M:N, mounted on a carrier when running
Stack OS-allocated, fixed-ish Heap objects (stack chunks), grows/shrinks
Creation cost ~tens of microseconds, MB-scale reserve ~hundreds of bytes to few KB initially
Scheduler OS JDK ForkJoinPool (FIFO mode)
Daemon configurable always daemon
Priority settable ignored (fixed at normal)
Pooling yes, normal no, one per task

When a virtual thread hits a blocking JDK call (socket read, BlockingQueue.take, Lock.lock, sleep), the JDK parks it: the stack is copied to the heap, the carrier is freed and picks the next runnable virtual thread. When the I/O is ready the virtual thread is resubmitted to the scheduler. Cost of a blocked virtual thread is just its heap-resident stack, so 1M of them is a heap question, not an OS question.

 100k virtual threads (mostly parked, stacks on heap)
        |  mount / unmount
        v
 [carrier-1][carrier-2]...[carrier-N]   N = cores by default
        |
        v
      OS threads / CPU cores

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Thread vt = Thread.ofVirtual().name("order-", 0).start(() -> handle());
vt.join();
System.out.println(vt.isVirtual()); // true

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Virtual threads are green threads, same as Java 1.1." Different: they are scheduled onto OS threads in parallel and integrated with blocking JDK APIs.
  • Thinking they make CPU work faster. They do not; throughput improves only when threads spend time blocked.
  • Calling setPriority or expecting setDaemon(false) to do anything.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a virtual thread run on multiple cores at once? → Yes: many virtual threads are mounted on different carriers concurrently; parallelism is bounded by the carrier count (default = available processors).
  2. Do synchronized, Thread.currentThread(), ThreadLocal still work? → Yes, same API; synchronized has pinning caveats before Java 24 (see Q203/Q205).
  3. How does a stack live on the heap and not blow GC? → Frames are copied lazily into StackChunk objects when unmounting; only changed frames are copied on re-mount, and chunks are ordinary GC-managed objects.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "lightweight threads, millions possible". Senior: states the mount/unmount mechanism, that gain is capacity not speed (Little's law: concurrency = throughput x latency), that carriers default to core count, and that the heap now carries the thread-cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that flipped to virtual threads and saw no latency win were CPU-bound all along; those with 200-thread Tomcat pools stuck behind slow downstreams saw the real gain.

questions.promptHtml: What are the ways to create and run virtual threads in Java 21, and which would you use in a service?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic API fluency, and whether you know the executor is not a pool.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Thread.ofVirtual().start(r) or Thread.startVirtualThread(r) for a single one, Thread.ofVirtual().factory() when a library wants a ThreadFactory, and Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() for services. That executor starts a fresh virtual thread per submitted task; it's not a pool, and since Java 19 ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, so try-with-resources waits for tasks."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Thread.ofVirtual() returns a Thread.Builder.OfVirtual; .name(prefix, start) gives numbered names. Virtual threads have an empty name by default, which hurts thread dumps and logs, so always name them.
  • Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(r) then start() if you need to configure before running.
  • Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(factory) generalises it.
  • close() on the executor blocks until all submitted tasks finish (it calls shutdown then awaitTermination), which makes fan-out scoped.
  • Frameworks: Spring Boot 3.2+ with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true, Tomcat and Jetty have virtual-thread executors; usually you don't create them by hand.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    List<Future<String>> fs = urls.stream()
        .map(u -> exec.submit(() -> httpGet(u)))
        .toList();
    for (var f : fs) results.add(f.get()); // blocks cheaply
} // close() waits for all tasks

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping it in your own bounded pool "to be safe": Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()) rebuilds the old limit and defeats the point (but does not pool threads, just caps them; use a Semaphore instead, Q216).
  • Forgetting to name threads.
  • Using Executors.newCachedThreadPool and assuming it is virtual; it is not.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can I shutdownNow() the per-task executor? → Yes, it interrupts running virtual threads; cooperation still required.
  2. How do you make a @Async method use virtual threads in Spring? → Provide a TaskExecutor/AsyncTaskExecutor backed by virtual threads; Boot 3.2 wires this when the property is on.
  3. Thread.startVirtualThread vs builder? → Same result; the builder lets you name, set uncaught handler and inheritable-thread-local behavior.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the API. Senior adds: unnamed threads are an observability trap, the executor is closeable and scopes lifetime, and you bound concurrency by resource (Semaphore), not by threads.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An unnamed-virtual-thread fleet made logs useless until a team set Thread.ofVirtual().name("req-", 0)/MDC request IDs.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how virtual threads are scheduled: what are carrier threads and continuations, and what happens when a virtual thread blocks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who memorised "lightweight" from those who can debug a stuck carrier.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Each virtual thread is a continuation, a stack of frames that can be suspended and resumed, plus a scheduler. The scheduler is a FIFO-mode ForkJoinPool of platform threads called carriers, parallelism defaulting to the CPU count. A virtual thread is mounted on a carrier to run; when it blocks in a JDK API it yields, its frames go to the heap, the carrier is freed, and when it's unblocked it's resubmitted to the pool, possibly resuming on a different carrier."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Carrier = the platform thread currently executing the virtual thread. Thread.currentThread() returns the virtual thread, not the carrier; carrier is hidden from user code.
  • Scheduler tunables (JEP 444 / JDK docs): jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism (default = available processors), jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize (the scheduler may temporarily exceed parallelism, up to this max, to compensate for some blocking operations; default not stated in the JEP page, I recall 256, verify). It is separate from the common pool used by parallel streams.
  • Yielding points: JDK blocking primitives (LockSupport.park, socket I/O via NIO-based implementations, Thread.sleep, BlockingQueue, Lock, Semaphore). The scheduler is not preemptive: a virtual thread in a tight CPU loop is never time-sliced out; it holds its carrier until it blocks.
  • Some operations cannot unmount: file I/O on most platforms blocks the carrier (the runtime may add a temporary compensating carrier); pinned cases (Q203).
VT-A runs on C1 -> socket.read() would block
  -> park: copy frames to heap StackChunk, C1 free
  -> C1 takes VT-B from the scheduler queue
  ... data arrives -> VT-A resubmitted -> may resume on C2

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Observe carrier in toString (JDK prints VirtualThread[#22]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3)
Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread()));

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming time slicing: 8 CPU-spinning virtual threads on an 8-core box starve everything else (Q215).
  • Setting maxPoolSize huge to "fix" pinning; it doesn't compensate for pinned threads in 21.
  • Using Thread.currentThread() identity as carrier identity in thread-affinity caches.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why FIFO instead of FJP's usual LIFO? → Fairness among runnable virtual threads, since tasks are resumptions of long-lived threads, not forked subtasks.
  2. Can a virtual thread migrate between carriers? → Yes on every resume, which is why you can't rely on carrier-local state.
  3. Can I plug in my own scheduler? → Not in the public API in 21; there are internal/reflective hooks, unsupported.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "JVM schedules them". Senior: non-preemptive, FIFO FJP, parallelism = cores, what compensates and what doesn't, and why CPU hogs are the failure mode.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Latency-sensitive endpoints stalled when a handler hashed large payloads in a loop without yielding, because it sat on a carrier.

questions.promptHtml: For which workloads do virtual threads improve throughput, and for which do they not? Quantify it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests Little's law reasoning instead of cargo-culting.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "They help when concurrency is limited by threads blocked on I/O. Concurrency L = throughput x latency, so if each request waits 200 ms and I want 5,000 RPS I need 1,000 requests in flight; with 200 platform threads I cap at 1,000 RPS. Virtual threads remove that cap. For CPU-bound work, throughput is limited by cores, so they add nothing and can hurt."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Little's law: L = lambda x W. Example: 5,000 RPS x 0.2 s = 1,000 concurrent. A 200-thread pool gives max 200 / 0.2 = 1,000 RPS; the 16-core CPU is 10% used. Virtual threads let all 1,000 (or 10,000) wait concurrently.
  • CPU-bound: with C cores, a pool of ~C threads already saturates; extra virtual threads only add queueing. Use a ForkJoinPool/fixed pool sized to cores.
  • Mixed: each request = 5 ms CPU + 200 ms waiting. CPU capacity = 16 cores / 5 ms = 3,200 RPS; waiting capacity unbounded. Thread cost was the bottleneck, now CPU is.
  • Downstream limits remain: virtual threads shift the bottleneck to DB pool, connection limits, rate limits; you now need explicit bounds (Q216).
  • JDK docs: unlikely to benefit if you never reach ~10,000 concurrent tasks (rule of thumb from the docs).
  • Latency per request does not improve; throughput and capacity do.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: none needed (arithmetic above).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Benchmarking a CPU-only endpoint and concluding "no gain, Loom is hype".
  • Ignoring that more concurrency melts the DB (Q202).
  • Using virtual threads for a long-running CPU-parallel pipeline.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A service handles 300 RPS at 50 ms. Benefit? → L = 15 concurrent; negligible, don't migrate for this.
  2. What about fan-out of 20 parallel calls per request? → Good fit: cheap threads per subcall (with structured concurrency, Q208).
  3. Does it help a Redis client using one multiplexed connection? → Only marginally; the multiplexing already solved the concurrency problem.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "good for I/O". Senior: computes L, identifies the new bottleneck, and says what stays unchanged (latency, CPU).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team raising Tomcat max threads from 200 to 2,000 platform threads saw memory climb; virtual threads gave the same capacity at far lower footprint, but their DB pool of 20 became the wall.

questions.promptHtml: Why is pooling virtual threads an anti-pattern, and how do you limit concurrency instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Pools were the central pattern for 20 years; this checks you unlearned it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A pool exists to amortise the cost of an expensive resource and to cap how many exist. Virtual threads are cheap, so there's nothing to amortise, and pooling them also reintroduces queueing where a task waits for a free slot instead of just blocking cheaply. If I need to cap concurrent access to a resource, I use a Semaphore around the call, sized to the resource, not to the thread."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• JEP 444 and the docs state: do not pool virtual threads; create one per task. A thread is the unit of a task now, like an object.
  • A fixed pool couples two unrelated things: "how many tasks may run" and "how many threads exist". Semaphore separates them: unlimited threads, limited permits for a scarce resource (DB connections, a rate-limited API, memory-heavy step).
  • Semaphore is fair if constructed so (new Semaphore(n, true)), and parked virtual threads are cheap to queue, whereas a pool's BlockingQueue holds task objects with unbounded or rejecting semantics.
  • Per-resource semaphores compose: a per-downstream limit, a global limit.
  • Also remove pools that exist only to give threads a "nice name" or to cache objects in ThreadLocals.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private final Semaphore payments = new Semaphore(50); // provider allows 50 concurrent

String charge(Order o) throws InterruptedException {
    payments.acquire();
    try { return client.charge(o); }  // blocking call
    finally { payments.release(); }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• newFixedThreadPool(10, virtualFactory): serialises, no benefit.
  • Acquiring the permit and forgetting finally, leaking permits until total stall.
  • Using the semaphore to bound CPU work.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you put the semaphore: before or after queueing? → At the call site wrapping the scarce call; requests wait cheaply there.
  2. How do you add a timeout? → tryAcquire(timeout, unit) and fail fast with a 503/bulkhead exception.
  3. What about unbounded virtual threads and memory? → Each parked thread holds its stack plus captured request data; bound intake (admission control) before the virtual threads pile up.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "don't pool them". Senior: separates "number of threads" from "number of permits", adds timeouts/shedding, and monitors waiting count.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team capped 5,000 virtual threads via a fixed pool, recreating the exact queueing they were escaping; replacing with per-dependency semaphores restored p99.

questions.contextHtml: An order service runs Spring Boot 3.2 on Java 21 with Tomcat, 200 threads, a HikariCP pool of 30 connections (maximumPoolSize=30), p99 180 ms at 800 RPS. Marketing expects 8x traffic. A teammate enables spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true and load tests at 6,000 RPS. Results: CPU 35%, pod memory fine, but p99 jumps to 11 s, and logs show HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms (and some 5xx at the gateway). Each request does 2 queries, 15 ms each, in one transaction.
questions.promptHtml: The feature "worked" but the system is worse. Explain why and what you change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Virtual threads aren't ready, turn them off" or "raise the Hikari pool to 600". The first ignores that 200 platform threads were acting as an accidental limiter; the second overloads the database.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the DB's max connections and CPU? (is 30 per pod x pods near the limit?) How many pods? Is Hikari the only gate? Are requests transactional for their whole lifetime? Is there client-side timeout/retry at the gateway (amplification)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the property or cap in-flight requests with a servlet filter/semaphore at ~60 until a proper fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Hikari pool is the true bottleneck, 6,000 RPS needs L = 6,000 x 0.03 s = 180 busy connections vs 30 available; (b) previously Tomcat's 200 threads throttled arrivals so excess queued in the accept queue, now all requests are in flight and all queue on Hikari; (c) long transactions hold connections while waiting on other IO; (d) retries multiplying load; red herring: CPU 35% is not evidence of anything wrong with the JVM.
  4. How I'd verify each: Micrometer hikaricp.connections.pending/active/usage, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json to see thousands of virtual threads parked in HikariPool.getConnection; DB pg_stat_activity/SHOW PROCESSLIST; JFR.
  5. Root cause: Virtual threads removed the implicit concurrency cap. The real constraint (30 connections = max throughput 30 / 0.03 s = 1,000 RPS) was always there; now excess demand waits 30 s on the pool instead of waiting in Tomcat's queue, so timeout and queue time dominate the tail.
  6. Fix: Short-term: admission control: a Semaphore (or reject with 429/503) at the edge sized near pool capacity; fail fast with shorter connectionTimeout (e.g. 500 ms-2 s). Long-term: reduce DB time per request (batch, cache, shorter transactions), scale DB/pods, size pool via measured DB capacity (e.g. 60 total across pods), add read replicas.
  7. Prevention: Load test at 2x peak with virtual threads; dashboard on pending connections; alert on Hikari wait time; review checklist: every scarce downstream has an explicit bound.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Won't raise Hikari to 600 (DB thrash); won't keep platform threads as the throttle (accidental limits are untunable).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if a bulkhead rejects 20% at peak? → Acceptable and intentional; better than 11 s tail; add autoscaling and retries with jitter on the client.
  • Would reactive R2DBC change this? → The pool limit still exists; async doesn't create DB capacity.
  • Can virtual threads help at all here? → Yes for the non-DB waiting (HTTP calls), as long as DB use is bounded.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found that for years their 200-thread cap had silently protected a Postgres primary; the day concurrency was freed, the DB hit its connection limit and took down unrelated services sharing it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames Loom or just raises the pool.
  • Hire: identifies Hikari as bottleneck via Little's law and adds a bound.
  • Strong hire: also explains the accidental-limiter effect, fail-fast timeouts, load shedding and DB-side capacity maths.

questions.promptHtml: What is virtual thread pinning in Java 21, what causes it, and why does it matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the number-one production gotcha of Loom; interviewers want mechanism plus diagnosis.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Pinning means a virtual thread can't unmount from its carrier while blocked. In Java 21 that happens when it blocks inside a synchronized block or method, or inside a native method or foreign function frame. The carrier OS thread is then blocked too, and the scheduler doesn't add carriers to compensate. A few pinned threads waiting on slow I/O can consume all carriers and stall the whole app even though CPU is idle."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Unmounting requires copying the virtual thread's frames to the heap. In 21, a monitor held via synchronized was owned by the carrier OS thread, and native frames can't be copied, so the continuation couldn't yield. Result: park degrades into blocking the carrier.

Pinning is only a problem when it is long and frequent: a synchronized block guarding an in-memory counter is fine; a synchronized method wrapping a JDBC call or HTTP request is not. With N carriers (default = cores, e.g. 8), 8 virtual threads blocked in pinned I/O means zero other virtual threads run. JEP 444 notes the scheduler does not compensate for pinning by growing parallelism.

Typical hidden culprits: older JDBC drivers and libraries using synchronized around socket I/O, logging appenders, Object.wait(), class initialisers. The Object.wait() call pinned in 21 too.

Diagnostics (21): -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full|short prints stacks when a thread blocks while pinned; JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned (on by default, 20 ms threshold).

Fix: replace synchronized around blocking work with ReentrantLock, or upgrade to a library version that did; or upgrade to Java 24+ (Q205).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Pins on Java 21 when the call blocks
synchronized (lockObj) { frequentIO(); }

// Does not pin
lock.lock();
try { frequentIO(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Replacing every synchronized with ReentrantLock blindly; only blocking-while-held matters.
  • Assuming maxPoolSize rescues you; compensation applies to some blocking ops, not pinned ones.
  • Forgetting that third-party code you don't control can pin.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a pinned thread break correctness? → No, only scalability.
  2. How would you find pinning in production on 21? → JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events with stack traces, or tracePinnedThreads in staging.
  3. Is ReentrantLock safe from pinning for everything? → It parks via LockSupport, which unmounts; but any native frame on the stack still pins.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "synchronized is bad with Loom". Senior: only blocking-while-holding, with N-carrier arithmetic, native frames too, diagnosis tools, and that Java 24 changes it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A JDBC driver using synchronized on its connection stalled an 8-core pod at 8 concurrent slow queries while CPU read 5%.

questions.contextHtml:
A notification service (Java 21, Spring Boot 3.2, virtual threads on, 4 vCPU pods, 6 replicas) calls an internal REST API. After a release, p99 goes from 120 ms to 9 s every few minutes, then recovers; CPU ~8%; heap flat at 40%. Thread dumps via jstack show only ~14 platform threads. Log excerpt every spike: Request timed out waiting for response from the gateway. The release added a "rate-limit shim":

class ShimClient {
    private final HttpClientWrapper http;
    synchronized Response call(Request r) {   // "to keep it simple and ordered"
        return http.send(r);                  // network call, 50 ms normally, 3 s when downstream is slow
    }
}

Red herring: a recent GC flag change.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without taking the service down.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the replica count or heap" or blaming GC. It misses that the symptom is idle CPU plus stalled throughput, a scheduling signature, not a resource one.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the spikes begin with the release? Are all pods affected, or only pods calling the slow downstream? What do JFR / jdk.tracePinnedThreads show? Is the shim called on every request?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the shim, or temporarily set -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism higher? No, that doesn't help pinned waits meaningfully; rollback is correct. If rollback is slow, route traffic away from pods during slow-downstream windows.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) synchronized + network I/O pins carriers; with 4 carriers, 4 blocked calls in the monitor path occupy every carrier (and also serialises calls through one monitor); (b) downstream slowness is the trigger; (c) connection pool issue; (d) GC (red herring: heap flat, no pauses in -Xlog:gc*).
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> JFR.start then look at jdk.VirtualThreadPinned (20 ms default) with stack pointing to ShimClient.call; jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json to see virtual threads blocked on the monitor; jstack shows carrier ForkJoinPool-1-worker-N threads stuck in socket read.
  5. Root cause: One global monitor serialises calls (throughput = 1 / latency, so 3 s downstream means 0.33 RPS), and while a virtual thread waits for or holds that monitor on Java 21 it pins its carrier. With 4 carriers all pinned, every other request (even ones that never touch the shim) cannot run.
  6. Fix: Short-term: remove the shim or replace with ReentrantLock (or better, no lock; rate limiting via Semaphore/token bucket, see Q216). Long-term: upgrade to Java 24+ where JEP 491 lets virtual threads release carriers while blocked on monitors; still drop the serialisation unless ordering is a hard requirement.
  7. Prevention: Alert on JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned; staging soak with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short; code-review rule "no blocking call inside synchronized in request path"; synthetic slow-downstream test.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Won't just bump maxPoolSize or carriers (masks, burns memory); won't convert everything to ReentrantLock blindly; keep synchronized for tiny in-memory sections.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same code on Java 25, does it still stall? → Carrier pinning disappears, but the single monitor still serialises calls; throughput stays 1/latency (Q205).
  • How do you keep ordering without a lock? → Single-consumer queue or per-key serial executor.
  • Why does CPU show 8%? → Carriers are blocked, not computing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident had a legacy "audit sink" with a synchronized write() that did fsync; under Loom the 4-carrier pod froze during disk latency spikes, with every health check also failing since probes ran on the same scheduler.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: GC or capacity guesses.
  • Hire: identifies pinning via synchronized+IO and fixes with ReentrantLock/rollback.
  • Strong hire: also notes serialisation vs pinning, Java 24 behavior, JFR evidence, and health-check collateral damage.

questions.promptHtml: What changed for pinning in Java 24, and what pinning remains?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests currency; stale "synchronized always pins" is a common mid-level answer.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "JEP 491, delivered in Java 24, lets virtual threads acquire, hold and release monitors independently of their carrier, so a virtual thread can unmount while blocked inside synchronized, while waiting to enter a monitor, and in Object.wait(). Pinning remains for native frames: native methods or FFM calls that call back into Java and block, plus blocking during class loading or class initialisation. jdk.tracePinnedThreads no longer works; the JFR pinning event stays for the remaining cases."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Before 24: monitor ownership tied to the carrier OS thread. After: monitors are owned by the virtual thread, so the JVM can park it and run another on the carrier.
  • Remaining (per JEP 491): (1) native frames on the stack when blocking, e.g. JNI up-call that blocks, FFM upcall; (2) blocking during class loading while resolving a symbolic reference; (3) blocking inside a class initialiser (<clinit>); (4) waiting for another thread's class initialisation. The JDK team considers 2-4 rarely problematic.
  • jdk.tracePinnedThreads is stated to be removed/ineffective; jdk.VirtualThreadPinned remains and is to be enhanced to report reason and carrier.
  • What does not change: a synchronized block still gives mutual exclusion, so a long I/O inside it still serialises all callers. Pinning fix does not fix contention.
  • Practical: on 21 (LTS) you still need the ReentrantLock workaround; 25 is the next LTS and carries the fix (JEP 491 shipped in 24, so it is in 25; confirm in your vendor's release notes).
Java 21:   synchronized{ blockingIO } -> carrier blocked (pinned)
Java 24+:  synchronized{ blockingIO } -> VT unmounts; monitor still held; others queue on monitor

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Java 25: no carrier pinned, but still serialised
synchronized (this) { return http.send(req); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Java 24 fixed everything": native frames and class-init remain.
  • Removing ReentrantLock migration prematurely when still on 21 LTS.
  • Believing monitors no longer contend.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Object.wait() pin in 24? → No, it can unmount.
  2. A JNI library calls back to Java that blocks; pinned? → Yes (native frame).
  3. How would you detect the remaining cases? → JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned (with reason, per JEP, enhanced).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE repeats "synchronized pins". Senior: version-aware, knows remaining cases, and separates pinning (scheduling) from contention (design).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams on 21 LTS kept workarounds; after moving to 25 they deleted shims but discovered contention they had previously blamed on pinning.

questions.contextHtml:
A service migrated to virtual threads (Java 21, one virtual thread per request, ~20,000 concurrent at peak). Code:

public class Formatter {
    private static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> FMT =
        ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss"));

    private static final ThreadLocal<byte[]> BUF =
        ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new byte[256 * 1024]); // "avoid allocation per request"

    static String fmt(Date d) { return FMT.get().format(d); }
}

After the move, heap usage rises from 1.5 GB to 6 GB at peak, GC allocation rate triples, and p99 worsens. A tester notes MDC context sometimes appears in logs of other requests only when they use a hand-rolled platform worker pool.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ThreadLocals are not supported with virtual threads." They are supported. The weak answer also misses the numbers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a virtual thread created per request? Does anything pool or reuse them? Which ThreadLocals exist (heap dump)? Is the 256 KB buffer needed per call?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop the BUF thread local first (largest); shrink or allocate per call.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) per-thread caches multiply by thread count: 20,000 x 256 KB = 5 GB, matching the heap jump (6 GB - 1.5 GB = 4.5 GB, in the same ballpark); (b) SimpleDateFormat per virtual thread: allocation churn since each short-lived thread builds a new one, no reuse; (c) inheritable thread locals copying; red herring: MDC leakage in a hand-rolled pool, which is a separate classic bug.
  4. How I'd verify: heap dump + MAT: dominator tree by ThreadLocalMap entries; -Djdk.traceVirtualThreadLocals=true (staging) prints a stack trace when a virtual thread sets a thread local; JFR allocation profiling.
  5. Root cause: ThreadLocal caching assumed few long-lived threads reusing the value. With a virtual thread per task, there is no reuse: every request pays creation, and N concurrent threads hold N copies.
  6. Fix: Use immutable thread-safe DateTimeFormatter (static final, no ThreadLocal). Allocate buffers per call (young-gen cheap) or use a bounded pool / ThreadLocal only when the object is expensive AND threads are long-lived (platform worker threads for CPU work). Pass request context with ScopedValue where available (Q207).
  7. Prevention: Lint rule/ArchUnit against static ThreadLocal caches; heap budget review; load test at peak thread count.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Won't disable thread locals globally (libraries use them); won't reintroduce pooling just for the buffer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is MDC safe on virtual threads? → Yes per-thread, but it won't propagate to other executors; copy explicitly.
  • Does InheritableThreadLocal cost more? → Yes, children copy values at creation; avoid with many threads.
  • Can you opt out? → Thread.Builder.allowSetThreadLocals(false) exists on the builder, making set throw; use only for strict code.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found a library caching a 64 KB Cipher buffer per thread; at 50k virtual threads it was a 3 GB surprise that the heap dump found in ten minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: says ThreadLocal unsupported.
  • Hire: ties per-thread caches to thread count and moves to immutable/shared objects.
  • Strong hire: quantifies, uses MAT and jdk.traceVirtualThreadLocals, mentions ScopedValue and MDC propagation.

questions.promptHtml: What is ScopedValue, how does it differ from ThreadLocal, and what is its status across Java versions?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know the intended replacement for passing context to many threads and the status caveats.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A ScopedValue is an immutable binding that is visible only for the dynamic extent of a run/call, and is inherited by structured-concurrency child threads without copying. There's no set, so no mutation from callees and no leaks beyond the scope. It was preview in 21 (JEP 446), refined through 22-24, and finalised in Java 25 (JEP 506). Reading is usually as cheap as a local variable."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• ThreadLocal: mutable, lifetime tied to the thread (leaks in pools), inheritable ones are copied into each child, so memory grows with thread count.
  • ScopedValue: ScopedValue.where(KEY, v).run(() -> ...) binds for the lambda; KEY.get() reads; isBound() checks; call returns a result. Nested rebinding is allowed and shadows only within the inner scope.
  • Child threads forked via StructuredTaskScope see the parent's bindings automatically; ForkJoinPool doesn't support the inheritance (JEP 506), so don't assume it in parallel streams. Plain Thread/executors don't inherit either.
  • In JEP 506 final, the one API change was that orElse no longer accepts null.
  • Use cases: request ID, authenticated principal, tenant, transaction context.
  • Not a drop-in: frameworks still use ThreadLocal (Spring's RequestContextHolder, MDC); migrate at your own boundaries.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
static final ScopedValue<String> REQ_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance();

void handle(Request r) {
    ScopedValue.where(REQ_ID, r.id()).run(() -> service.process()); // JDK 25 final
}
String id() { return REQ_ID.get(); } // throws NoSuchElementException if unbound

(On Java 21-24 it needs --enable-preview.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it expecting mutation or a per-thread cache.
  • Expecting inheritance in a normal ExecutorService.
  • Using on 21 without --enable-preview, or shipping preview to production unknowingly.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why immutable? → Predictable one-way data flow and bounded lifetime; enables cheap implementation and no leak.
  2. How to "change" a value for a callee? → Rebind in a nested where(...).run.
  3. Migration plan from MDC? → Bind at the entry, populate MDC from it at logging boundaries; keep MDC for logging libraries.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "new ThreadLocal". Senior: lifetime/immutability model, structured-concurrency inheritance, version status, and framework reality.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Context leaking across requests in thread pools (stale tenant ID) is the bug class it eliminates.

questions.promptHtml: What is structured concurrency, what problem does StructuredTaskScope solve, and what is its status?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you reason about task lifetimes, cancellation and error propagation, not just "spawn threads".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Structured concurrency says subtasks must finish within the scope that started them, like block-structured code. StructuredTaskScope forks subtasks as virtual threads, the owner joins, and on exit all children are done, so there are no leaked threads. With a fail-fast policy a failure cancels siblings and propagates. It is still a preview API: previewed from 21, with Java 25 delivering its fifth preview (JEP 505), where the API moved to StructuredTaskScope.open() plus Joiner policies. So use it behind --enable-preview, and never assume the 21 API compiles on 25."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Problem with ExecutorService/CompletableFuture fan-out: if one subtask fails, siblings keep running (wasted work, leaked threads); cancel propagation is manual; thread dumps don't show who owns whom; the parent can finish while children run.

Structured model: scope is AutoCloseable; close() ensures all forks end; children inherit ScopedValue bindings; thread dumps can show parent-child relationships.

Java 21 preview API: new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure() / ShutdownOnSuccess<T>, scope.fork(callable) returns Subtask<T>, scope.join() (or joinUntil(deadline)), then throwIfFailed(), then subtask.get(). Java 25 preview (JEP 505): StructuredTaskScope.open() (wait for all, fail if any fails) or open(Joiner) with Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow(), allSuccessfulOrThrow(), awaitAll(), allUntil(...); a configuration overload sets name, timeout, thread factory. The JEP also lists a sixth preview (JEP 525) as follow-up; verify which release you target.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Java 21 preview (--enable-preview)
try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
    var user  = scope.fork(() -> userSvc.get(id));
    var prefs = scope.fork(() -> prefSvc.get(id));
    scope.join().throwIfFailed();       // join first, then read
    return new Profile(user.get(), prefs.get());
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling subtask.get() before join() (throws IllegalStateException).
  • Treating it as GA in production without enabling preview deliberately.
  • Forking from a thread that isn't the scope owner (not allowed).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Difference from invokeAll? → Cancellation policies, inheritance of scoped values, observability, and no leakage guarantees.
  2. How do you set a deadline? → joinUntil in 21; timeout via config in the 25 API.
  3. What if I can't use preview? → Executor-per-task in try-with-resources plus manual cancel; Kotlin coroutineScope is the shipping analogue (A1).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "a nicer way to run tasks in parallel". Senior: lifetime guarantees, cancellation semantics, API instability across previews, and a fallback plan.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Leaked fan-out tasks hammering a degraded downstream after the request had already timed out is the incident this prevents.

questions.contextHtml:
A profile endpoint (Java 21 with --enable-preview, ~900 RPS) fans out to three services. A reviewer approves this code; in staging it throws intermittently and, when a downstream fails, latency is ~2 s longer than expected:

Profile load(String id) throws Exception {
    try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
        var user   = scope.fork(() -> userSvc.get(id));      // 30 ms
        var orders = scope.fork(() -> orderSvc.get(id));     // 40 ms, fails fast on bad id
        var recs   = scope.fork(() -> recSvc.get(id));       // 2 s, slow
        var u = user.get();                                   // line A
        scope.join();
        scope.throwIfFailed();
        return new Profile(u, orders.get(), recs.get());
    }
}

Error in logs: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Owner did not join after forking subtasks. Red herring: recent upgrade of the HTTP client library.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and explain the observed behaviors.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase timeouts" or blaming the HTTP client. It misses the API contract (join before get).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which Java version/API shape (21 preview vs 25 open())? Is the exception always at line A? Is there a request deadline?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an outage; patch code and hotfix; meanwhile a feature flag back to the sequential path if it exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) user.get() called before join() violates the contract (the scope throws IllegalStateException for reading a result before join); (b) once joined correctly, ShutdownOnFailure cancels siblings when orders fails, but only if join() is reached promptly; reading values early blocks sequential semantics; (c) no deadline, so recs can hold 2 s; (d) red herring: HTTP client.
  4. How I'd verify: unit test with a failing stub; jcmd Thread.dump_to_file shows the fork hierarchy; add timing logs per subtask.
  5. Root cause: get() before join() is illegal because results are only guaranteed available after the join; the slow tail stems from missing deadline and, because the failure policy only acts at join, nothing cancels recs until the owner reaches join.
  6. Fix:
try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
    var user   = scope.fork(() -> userSvc.get(id));
    var orders = scope.fork(() -> orderSvc.get(id));
    var recs   = scope.fork(() -> recSvc.get(id));
    scope.joinUntil(Instant.now().plusMillis(800)); // deadline; TimeoutException -> degrade
    scope.throwIfFailed();
    return new Profile(user.get(), orders.get(), recs.get());
}

Make recs optional with a fallback if it is non-critical (use ShutdownOnSuccess/separate scope). On Java 25 preview use StructuredTaskScope.open() with a timeout config. 7. Prevention: Test failure and timeout paths; decide critical vs optional subtasks; lint/review checklist for scope contract; pin the Java version since preview APIs change. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Won't catch-and-ignore the IllegalStateException; won't wrap in CompletableFuture just to avoid preview if cancellation matters.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does failing orders interrupt recs? → Yes after join sees the failure under ShutdownOnFailure, subtasks are cancelled (interrupted); the HTTP call must be interruptible.
  • What if recs ignores interrupts? → Scope close waits for it; so use call timeouts at the client.
  • Can a subtask fork its own scope? → Yes, nested scopes; tree structure is the point.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team shipped fan-out with CompletableFuture; when the first call failed the other two kept hitting a struggling recommendation service for 30 s per request, adding to the outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot identify the contract error.
  • Hire: join-before-get, deadline, and cancellation behavior.
  • Strong hire: critical-vs-optional design, interrupt-ability of clients, preview API volatility.

questions.promptHtml: How do you enable virtual threads in a Spring Boot application on Tomcat, and what exactly changes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical migration knowledge; the property is one line but the consequences are not.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "On Java 21+ and Spring Boot 3.2+, set spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true. Boot then runs Tomcat (or Jetty) request handling on virtual threads and uses virtual threads for @Async/scheduled task executors it auto-configures. Each request gets its own virtual thread, so the 200-thread cap disappears. Everything downstream, notably the DB pool, still has its old limits."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Mechanism: Tomcat's connector executor becomes a per-task virtual-thread executor; Spring's applicationTaskExecutor becomes SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor with virtual threads (Boot docs; verify exact bean per Boot version).
  • server.tomcat.threads.max no longer bounds concurrency (check your Boot version docs for max-connections / accept-count semantic: server.tomcat.max-connections and accept-count still apply to connections).
  • Spring Framework 6.1+ / Boot 3.2 minimum. On Spring Boot 3.2.0 there were fixes around virtual-thread executors in later patch releases (verify) - use latest patch.
  • Pre-flight checklist: DB pool sizing, synchronized + blocking in your code and drivers (Java 21), ThreadLocal caches, per-thread assumptions (e.g. @Transactional binds to thread, fine), observability agents compatible, Netty/HTTP clients.
  • Non-Spring: Helidon Nima, Quarkus @RunOnVirtualThread, Micronaut thread.pool options.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# application.properties (Boot 3.2+, Java 21+)
spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true
@Bean
TomcatProtocolHandlerCustomizer<?> vt() { // manual equivalent
    return h -> h.setExecutor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor());
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Flipping the switch in prod without raising observability on Hikari wait time (Q202).
  • Assuming server.tomcat.threads.max still protects the service.
  • Leaving a CPU-heavy @Async on the same executor.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Spring WebFlux benefit? → No; it's non-blocking already; this is for MVC/blocking stacks.
  2. How would you keep a CPU-bound job separate? → A dedicated bounded platform executor.
  3. How do you roll it out safely? → Canary pod, flag via property, Q211.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: the property. Senior: the removed implicit limiter, downstream bounds, pinning and observability prerequisites.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Typical first incident after enabling: the DB or a downstream rate limit becomes the new wall.

questions.contextHtml: A payments-adjacent API (Java 17, Spring Boot 3.1, Tomcat 300 threads, 12 pods x 4 vCPU, 2,500 RPS total, p99 220 ms) must move to Java 21 + virtual threads to survive a 3x campaign without tripling pods. Dependencies: Postgres via HikariCP (20/pod; DB max_connections 400, shared with another service using 150), Redis, an old SOAP client library (synchronized internally), and a metrics agent that uses ThreadLocals. Error budget is tight, no downtime allowed.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the migration. What goes wrong, in what order do you de-risk it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Upgrade to 21 and set the property." No staged rollout, no capacity math, no rollback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 3x CPU-bound or I/O-bound (profile first)? DB headroom? Can the SOAP library be replaced? Is the agent virtual-thread-aware? How is rollback done (config vs image)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; prep step is a rollback switch: the property is a config flag, so rollback is a restart of canaries, not a redeploy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (risks): (a) DB: 12 pods x 20 = 240 + 150 = 390 of 400 connections, no headroom; more pods or larger pools will break it; (b) SOAP synchronized pins carriers on 21 (4 carriers per pod); (c) ThreadLocal agent/caches inflate memory; (d) CPU-bound hotspots (XML parsing) mean no gain; (e) older drivers/libs with pinning.
  4. How I'd verify: Step 1: upgrade to Java 21 platform threads alone (separate risk). Step 2: staging load test at 3x with JFR (jdk.VirtualThreadPinned, allocation), Micrometer hikari pending, Thread.dump_to_file. Step 3: 1 canary pod at 5% via weighted routing, compare p50/p99/errors/GC/DB connections for 24 h. Step 4: ramp 25/50/100%.
  5. Root cause (of the likely failure): Removing the implicit 300-thread limiter exposes the Hikari/DB limit and pinning in the SOAP client.
  6. Fix: Wrap the SOAP client in a ReentrantLock-based facade or isolate it on a bounded platform executor; add a Semaphore at the DB layer sized to ~20 plus short connectionTimeout; cap total DB connections via PgBouncer if pods scale; keep CPU hot path on a fixed pool.
  7. Prevention: Continuous JFR pinning alert, dashboards for virtual thread count (JFR/JMX not exposed by ThreadMXBean, see Q214), game day on slow downstream.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Won't change JDK version and threading model in one deploy; won't big-bang; won't raise pool sizes to "match" the new concurrency.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Canary looks better at p50 but p99 worse; why? → Probably queueing on a bounded resource; compare pending counts.
  • What if the agent can't be replaced? → Accept memory cost or run it only on platform executors; vendor upgrade.
  • Is going to Java 25 better than 21? → Removes synchronized pinning (JEP 491) but check vendor/frameworks support first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite migration hit 0 pinning on staging but production's slower real downstream triggered it; JFR in prod caught it in the canary stage, avoiding a full rollout.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flips switch everywhere.
  • Hire: stages rollout, checks pools and pinning, has rollback.
  • Strong hire: connection arithmetic, separates JDK upgrade from threading change, and defines canary metrics.

questions.promptHtml: Virtual threads vs reactive programming (WebFlux/Reactor): when would you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Architecture judgment; there is no single right answer, the reasoning is the signal.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Both solve 'too many threads blocked on I/O'. Reactive does it by never blocking: async pipelines, operators, backpressure, a few event-loop threads. Virtual threads keep blocking style and let the JVM do the multiplexing. For most CRUD and orchestration services I'd choose virtual threads: simpler code, normal stack traces, normal debugging, existing blocking libraries. I'd still choose reactive for streaming, backpressure-centric pipelines, or when the stack is already reactive and working."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Dimension Virtual threads Reactive
Code style imperative declarative operators
Debuggability normal stack traces assembly traces, hooks
Backpressure not built in (use Semaphore/bounded queues) first-class (Reactive Streams)
Ecosystem all blocking libs (JDBC) needs non-blocking drivers (R2DBC)
Memory per concurrent task stack on heap small state machine objects
CPU-bound / streaming no gain good for streaming/event pipelines
Learning curve low high
  • Reactive's strengths stay: composing event streams, SSE/websocket fan-out, flow control, huge fan-in with tiny memory per connection.
  • Mixed approach: don't block event-loop threads; don't call reactive APIs with .block() inside virtual threads unless intended.
  • Migration: existing WebFlux systems rarely justify a rewrite.
  • Compare costs: a million idle connections is heap for virtual threads vs tiny objects for Reactor.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Virtual-thread style orchestration: plain and debuggable
User u = userClient.get(id);           // blocks (cheap)
List<Order> os = orderClient.list(id); // blocks (cheap)
return assemble(u, os);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Virtual threads kill reactive." Backpressure and streaming remain reactive's domain.
  • Mixing: Mono.block() inside event loop threads.
  • Choosing by hype instead of team skills and the dominant workload.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you do backpressure with virtual threads? → Bounded queues, Semaphores, admission control, rate limits.
  2. What about R2DBC vs JDBC on virtual threads? → JDBC works with bounded pool; R2DBC if you need streaming result backpressure.
  3. Operational difference? → Virtual threads: thread dumps and profilers just work; reactive needs tracing/hooks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "VT simpler, reactive faster". Senior: workload-based decision, backpressure story, migration cost, and mixed-model hazards.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reactive service with mysterious blocked event-loop calls was cheaper to fix by moving the legacy part to virtual-thread MVC than by rewriting all clients.

questions.promptHtml: How do virtual threads compare to Kotlin coroutines, and could one replace the other on a server?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Kotlin shops need the nuance; also tests understanding of stackful vs stackless.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Virtual threads are stackful and runtime-level: any blocking JDK call can suspend, no language support needed, and existing blocking libraries benefit. Coroutines are stackless, compiled into state machines, with suspend colouring the call graph. Coroutines give structured concurrency, cancellation, Flow and multiplatform that are shipping and mature, while Loom's structured concurrency is still preview. On the server I wouldn't rewrite coroutine code to virtual threads; I'd use them side by side, and for new Java code virtual threads are the natural default. Coroutine mechanics belong to the Kotlin chunk."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Stackful vs stackless: virtual threads capture the real stack at any depth; coroutines suspend only at suspend points, so non-suspend blocking calls block the underlying dispatcher thread.
  • Coroutines: cooperative cancellation built in, scopes and withTimeout, Flow with backpressure, context propagation via CoroutineContext.
  • Virtual threads: cancellation via interrupt only; structured concurrency API still preview (Q208).
  • Interop: Dispatchers.IO can be backed by a virtual-thread executor (Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()); pinning issues apply to blocking calls inside.
  • Allocation: coroutine frames are heap objects per suspension; virtual thread stack chunks copy on yield. Both cheap at server scale.
  • Pitfall: calling blocking code in coroutines on Dispatchers.Default starves it; virtual threads tolerate blocking by design.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val vtDispatcher = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()
suspend fun load(): String = withContext(vtDispatcher) { blockingJdbcCall() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming blocking inside a coroutine is free because "Loom exists".
  • Rewriting a stable coroutine service for fashion.
  • Forgetting that ThreadLocal context does not follow coroutines automatically.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Function colouring? → Coroutines have it (suspend), virtual threads don't.
  2. Cancellation on client disconnect? → Coroutines propagate; virtual threads need interrupt wiring (framework dependent).
  3. Which uses less memory per task? → Coroutines usually less; virtual threads are close enough for typical server loads (verify with a benchmark).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "VT is Java's coroutines". Senior: stackful vs stackless, cancellation/structure maturity gap, interop and migration stance.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Kotlin team with blocking JDBC in Dispatchers.Default fixed starvation with a bounded dedicated dispatcher rather than a full virtual-thread rewrite.

questions.contextHtml: A Java 21 service on virtual threads hangs for ~40 s at a time: health checks time out, RPS drops to near zero, CPU 3%. On-call runs jstack <pid> and sees only ~25 platform threads (ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1..4 carriers, GC threads, Tomcat acceptor) and no application stack traces. They conclude "nothing is running" and want to restart. Metrics from ThreadMXBean.getThreadCount() also show ~25 threads while the access log shows ~6,000 in-flight requests.
questions.promptHtml: How do you see what the virtual threads are doing, and what tooling do you rely on?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart it, jstack shows nothing wrong." That discards the evidence and misses that standard dumps and MXBeans do not list virtual threads.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is JFR available/continuous? Is the pod still alive for a dump? Did this start after enabling virtual threads or a release?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Take evidence before restarting: jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/td.json (does not pause the app per JEP 444), and a short JFR; then restart one pod, leave others if safe.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) carriers pinned/blocked (look at the 4 carrier threads' stacks in jstack for socket reads or monitor waits); (b) all virtual threads waiting on a scarce resource (Hikari, Semaphore, lock); (c) downstream hang with no timeout; (d) GC (red herring: check -Xlog:gc*).
  4. How I'd verify: the JSON dump groups virtual threads by stack; count how many share the same top frame. JFR: jdk.VirtualThreadPinned (on by default, 20 ms), jdk.VirtualThreadSubmitFailed; jdk.VirtualThreadStart/End are off by default, enable them briefly. Remember ThreadMXBean and Thread.getAllStackTraces() cover platform threads only, and jdk.trackAllThreads=false can hide builder-created threads from dumps.
  5. Root cause (example outcome): 5,800 virtual threads parked in HikariPool.getConnection because a leaked connection (missing close) exhausted the pool; carriers were fine; jstack showed nothing because parked virtual threads are not platform threads.
  6. Fix: Fix the leak; set connectionTimeout; add leak detection (leakDetectionThreshold).
  7. Prevention: Continuous JFR; custom gauge for in-flight requests; alert on pool pending; runbook line "use Thread.dump_to_file for Loom services"; name virtual threads.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Won't enable jdk.traceVirtualThreadLocals/full trace flags in prod without a reason; won't rely on jstack alone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does findDeadlockedThreads() see virtual threads? → No (platform only, per JEP 444); use the JSON dump and analysis.
  • Why does the dump omit lock info? → The Thread.dump_to_file format omits object addresses and locks, among other things; correlate with JFR.
  • Can dumps be big? → Yes with 100k threads; group by stack.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team spent an hour staring at a clean jstack before someone remembered the JSON dump; 9,000 virtual threads were parked on one semaphore nobody released on an error path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts, says nothing is running.
  • Hire: knows Thread.dump_to_file and JFR pinning event.
  • Strong hire: knows MXBean/getAllStackTraces limits, groups stacks, links symptoms to a resource and captures evidence first.

questions.contextHtml: A document-processing API (Java 21, 8 vCPU pods, 10 pods) parses PDFs: per request ~400 ms of CPU (text extraction) plus 100 ms waiting on object storage. It was on a 64-thread platform pool; p99 was 1.4 s at 120 RPS/pod. To "save cost", the team moved all handling to newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Result: p50 doubled, p99 6 s, health-check endpoint (same scheduler) occasionally times out, throughput per pod unchanged at ~15 RPS (CPU 100%). Red herring: the object store SDK upgrade the same week.
questions.promptHtml: Why didn't virtual threads help, and why did latency get worse? What would you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Virtual threads should scale; tune parallelism up." Raising parallelism on a saturated CPU only adds contention.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the CPU-to-wait ratio per request? Is CPU at 100% before the change too? Is there backpressure at the load balancer? What are the SLOs for health checks?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert CPU stages to a fixed pool.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) work is CPU-bound: capacity = 8 cores / 0.4 s = 20 RPS max per pod (observed ~15, consistent); concurrency isn't the limiter; (b) with thousands of runnable virtual threads and a non-preemptive scheduler, each CPU stretch runs to completion on 8 carriers, so queueing delay grows and health checks queue behind them; (c) memory churn from many concurrent parses; (d) red herring: SDK.
  4. How I'd verify: Check CPU utilisation, JFR execution samples (parse dominating), async-profiler CPU flame graph, scheduler queue growth via runnable counts; compare arrival rate to 20 RPS/pod. Little's law: arrivals 120 RPS x 0.5 s = 60 in-flight, but only 8 can run CPU at a time.
  5. Root cause: The workload needs CPU, not threads. Switching removed the natural bounding (64 threads) and the fairness of OS time slicing; the virtual-thread scheduler is FIFO, non-preemptive, so latencies queue and tails explode.
  6. Fix: Keep virtual threads only for the 100 ms storage wait; run parsing on a bounded platform pool (e.g. 8-10 threads) with a bounded queue and 429/503 shedding; separate pool/priority for health checks; scale horizontally for CPU (120 RPS / 20 = 6+ pods at 100% CPU, so ~9-10 pods for headroom is about the current cost) or optimise parsing.
  7. Prevention: Load test with realistic CPU mix; define capacity per pod as cores / cpu-seconds-per-request; separate management port/executor.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Won't scale by lowering CPU limits; won't set parallelism > cores.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can a parse yield to others? → Not automatically; insert explicit Thread.yield() points only as a stopgap (verify behavior), better to isolate.
  • Does ForkJoinPool parallel stream help? → Only up to cores.
  • Why were we at 15 not 20 RPS? → GC, memory bandwidth, I/O, and the waiting portion.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team spent a quarter chasing "Loom regression" before computing cores / CPU-seconds and finding the old pool had been quietly doing admission control.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes parallelism up.
  • Hire: identifies CPU-bound and splits pools.
  • Strong hire: capacity maths, non-preemptive FIFO tail effect, health-check isolation and shedding.

questions.promptHtml: With virtual threads, thread count no longer limits you. How do you design backpressure and overload protection?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers know the limiter moved; they must put it somewhere deliberate.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I make limits explicit at three layers. At the edge, admission control caps in-flight requests (a Semaphore or concurrency limiter) and sheds excess with 429/503 quickly. Per dependency, a Semaphore bulkhead sized to what that dependency can take, with tryAcquire timeouts. And bounded queues wherever work is handed between stages. Plus timeouts on every outbound call, because a virtual thread waiting forever is a leak that holds memory."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Before: Tomcat's 200 threads + accept queue = implicit load shedding. After: unbounded thread creation; every overload converts to memory use and queueing inside the process, then timeouts.
  • Sizing a limit: L = lambda x W at target latency; pick the limit slightly above what the dependency sustains. E.g. DB with 30 connections and 15 ms queries sustains ~2,000 qps; cap queued waiters (e.g. 200) so the worst-case wait is 200 / 2,000 = 100 ms.
  • Adaptive limits (AIMD, Netflix-style concurrency-limits) adjust to observed latency; mention as an option, not default.
  • Fail fast vs queue: queue only if clients tolerate the wait; otherwise reject.
  • Memory: each in-flight request holds its stack plus buffers (say 50 KB-1 MB); 100k in-flight x 200 KB = 20 GB, so heap bounds concurrency; budget it.
  • Combine with Semaphore.tryAcquire(timeout), circuit breakers (Resilience4j) and deadline propagation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Bulkhead {
    private final Semaphore s;
    Bulkhead(int n) { s = new Semaphore(n); }
    <T> T call(Callable<T> c) throws Exception {
        if (!s.tryAcquire(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) throw new RejectedExecutionException("bulkhead full");
        try { return c.call(); } finally { s.release(); }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Unbounded intake relying on timeouts alone.
  • One global limit; one slow dependency starves the rest (need per-dependency).
  • Forgetting release on exceptions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you reject? → As early as possible (edge), before expensive work.
  2. Semaphore vs rate limiter? → Semaphore caps concurrency; rate limiter caps rate; use both when the provider limits RPS.
  3. How do you detect overload early? → Queue wait time and in-flight count metrics, not CPU alone.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "add a Semaphore". Senior: layered limits, math from Little's law, shedding policy, memory budget and metrics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The first Loom outages in many teams were not pinning but the missing limiter.

questions.promptHtml: True or false, and why: "Virtual threads make my code faster", "I should use them everywhere", "they replace ExecutorService".

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Quick filter for hype versus understanding.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "All three are false as stated. Virtual threads improve throughput for blocking I/O by allowing high concurrency; individual request latency doesn't drop. They shouldn't be used for CPU-bound work. And ExecutorService isn't replaced: I still use it, just with a per-task virtual-thread executor for blocking work and a fixed pool for CPU work."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Faster: the JDK docs say virtual threads offer scale, not speed; they increase throughput, not decrease latency.
  • Everywhere: CPU-bound loops, code with long pinned sections (Java 21), per-thread cached resources, and native-heavy code are poor fits.
  • ExecutorService: the abstraction remains; newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() is an ExecutorService. Parallel streams / ForkJoin remain for CPU parallelism.
  • Also false: "no more async code", "no need for timeouts/limits", "ThreadLocal is banned".
  • Another true one: you can mostly drop reactive for simple blocking orchestration (Q212).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ExecutorService io  = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();           // blocking I/O
ExecutorService cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()); // CPU work

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Measuring single-request latency to judge benefit.
  • Moving CPU-bound batch jobs to virtual threads.
  • Using virtual threads to "avoid thinking about limits".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What would you benchmark? → Throughput and tail latency at fixed concurrency far above the platform pool size, with a realistic I/O wait.
  2. Does synchronized still work? → Yes; pinning only matters for blocking within it on 21.
  3. Would you use them in a batch job? → If it's I/O fan-out yes; CPU-heavy no.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: parrots the hype or says "just threads". Senior: gives workload criteria and numbers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Wasted weeks on migrations of CPU-bound services yielding nothing.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review: an ingestion service (Java 21, 4 GB heap, container limit 6 GB, G1) was moved to a virtual thread per message. A downstream outage lasted 12 minutes. Messages kept arriving at 8,000/s from Kafka consumers that handed each message to executor.submit(...) on newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); each task did a HttpClient.send with the default (no) request timeout and held a 40 KB payload plus ~10 KB of stack. Timeline: heap rose from 1.2 GB to 4 GB in 6 minutes, GC pauses grew (Pause Young ... 450ms), then java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space, then the pod was restarted and reprocessed duplicates. Dashboards showed no thread-count growth (platform threads steady at 40).
questions.promptHtml: Run the review: what failed, why wasn't it visible, and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap to 8 GB." That only delays the OOM and ignores unbounded intake and the lack of timeouts.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What were consumer poll settings (max.poll.records, commit semantics)? What was the HTTP client timeout? Were metrics counting virtual threads? Was an OOM heap dump captured (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError)?
  2. Immediate mitigation (in the incident): Pause consumers (consumer.pause) or scale intake down; shed load; restart with a cap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) unbounded in-flight tasks: 8,000/s x 12 min x 60 = 5.76M tasks possible x 50 KB = ~288 GB if it ran unchecked; heap saturates in minutes (4 GB / (8,000 x 50 KB = 400 MB/s) is ~10 s of growth at full rate, so the observed 6 minutes implies a lower effective rate; either way, linear); (b) no timeouts, so tasks never end during the outage; (c) GC pressure due to live-set growth; (d) duplicates from uncommitted offsets on crash; red herring: platform thread count steady.
  4. How I'd verify: Heap dump in MAT: dominator tree shows VirtualThread/StackChunk and payload byte arrays; JFR jdk.VirtualThreadStart/End counts; -Xlog:gc* showing live set growth after full GCs; Kafka lag and consumer settings.
  5. Root cause: Backpressure was implicit in the old pool's bounded queue and thread count; virtual-thread-per-message removed it, and missing HTTP timeouts let tasks accumulate for the whole outage. Monitoring tracked platform threads, which hid the growth.
  6. Fix: Bound in-flight work with a Semaphore acquired before dispatch (consumer blocks, so Kafka backpressure applies; e.g. 500 permits x 50 KB = 25 MB); set connect/request timeouts (HttpRequest.timeout); idempotent processing and commit-after-process; circuit breaker around the downstream; metric for in-flight tasks.
  7. Prevention: Chaos test of 15-minute downstream outage; heap dump on OOM; alert on in-flight count and live set; review checklist: "what bounds intake?".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Won't just enlarge heap; won't drop messages silently; blocking the consumer thread on the Semaphore is deliberate backpressure, but keep poll interval (max.poll.interval.ms) in mind to avoid rebalances.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just a bounded queue? → Also valid; a Semaphore plus virtual threads keeps code simple, queue gives ordering/visibility.
  • Pause vs block? → Pausing partitions keeps the consumer in the group while blocking too long breaches the poll interval.
  • Duplicates? → At-least-once; need idempotency keys.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team's Loom migration passed all load tests because the downstream never failed; the first real outage found the unbounded memory path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raise heap/blame GC.
  • Hire: unbounded intake and missing timeout, adds Semaphore and timeouts.
  • Strong hire: quantifies memory per in-flight task, explains the observability blind spot, Kafka pause/poll interaction and idempotency.
